title: I know that my redeemer lives (Job 19:25–27)
hook: in the depths, Job reaches for hope anyway

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eliphaz and the comfort that hurt. Your line was don't explain their pain. Did you catch an at least before it left your mouth? Day four hundred forty-six.

By chapter nineteen, it's bad. The friends have stopped being gentle. Job says his brothers keep their distance, his servants ignore him, his breath is strange to his own wife, and little children mock him when he stands up. "Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me." Nobody does. And then he wishes for something odd. He wishes his words could be written down. Not just written: carved with an iron pen into rock, filled in with lead, so they'd last forever, so someone someday would know what he said. Here's the thing. His wish came true. What he says next is still read aloud and sung.
screen: `FRIENDS GONE, FAMILY DISTANT.` → `CARVE MY WORDS IN ROCK.` → `THE WISH CAME TRUE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth." The Hebrew word for redeemer is go'el. It isn't a church word first. It's a family word. In Israel, a go'el was your nearest relative with a duty to you. If you fell into debt and had to sell your land, your go'el bought it back. If you were sold into slavery, your go'el paid to free you. If you were killed, your go'el made sure your blood didn't go unanswered. In the book of Ruth, Boaz is the go'el who buys back a family's land and marries the widow Ruth. So when Job, abandoned by family and friends, says my go'el lives, he's saying: somebody is still on my side. Someone will stand up for me at the end, even if nobody here will. Who is it? Readers have heard it differently. Christian tradition hears Christ in this verse: the redeemer who lives and stands on the earth at the last day. Handel set it to music in Messiah, and the Book of Common Prayer sets it among the sentences that open its burial service. Jewish commentators have heard God himself as Job's defender. Some scholars think Job meant a heavenly witness, the advocate he mentions a few chapters earlier. And the next verse is hard to translate; it can be read as in my flesh shall I see God, or without my flesh. The King James Bible chose "yet in my flesh shall I see God." However it's read, a man at the bottom reaches up anyway.
screen: `GO'EL: THE FAMILY REDEEMER` · `BUYS BACK LAND, FREES THE SLAVE` · `CHRIST, GOD, OR A HEAVENLY WITNESS` · `A HOPE CARVED IN ROCK` · then, large: `I KNOW THAT MY REDEEMER LIVETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold on to one hope. Sit, and breathe. Think of one thing you're hoping for that you can't make happen yourself. Healing. A reconciliation. Someone coming home. Justice for something that went wrong. Name it to yourself plainly. Now hold it the way Job holds his: not because the evidence is good, but because you refuse to let go. If you pray, you can say his line slowly: I know that my redeemer liveth. If you don't, simply keep the hope in your hands for the whole sit, like something carved. The bell holds the time.
Redeemer. In Hebrew, go'el: the family member who buys back what was lost and stands up for you when no one else will.
Your line: my redeemer lives. Today, be someone's go'el in a small way. Stand up for one person who has nobody speaking for them. Day four hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Job 19:25 stands among the opening sentences of the Anglican burial service as a confession of hope in the resurrection, and it is sung as the soprano aria "I know that my Redeemer liveth" in Handel's Messiah.

original.note: Hebrew: my redeemer, from go'el, the kinsman who buys back and defends.
